items.q: Which big river flows through Hà Nội?
items.h: The Red River is named after its reddish-brown water, coloured by the mud it carries.

items.q: Which river flows through the old royal city of Huế?
items.h: The Perfume River is said to be named after flowers from orchards that drift into it.

items.q: Which city was Vietnam's capital under the Nguyễn emperors?
items.h: Huế was the capital from 1802 to 1945, and you can still walk round its Imperial City.

items.q: Which old Vietnamese town is famous for its glowing silk lanterns?
items.h: Hội An's old town is a World Heritage Site full of lantern shops and old wooden houses.

items.q: Đà Nẵng's Golden Bridge looks as if it is held by two giant what?
items.h: High in the Bà Nà Hills, the Golden Bridge seems to rest on two huge stone hands.

items.q: What is the highest mountain in Vietnam?
items.h: Fansipan, near Sa Pa, is over 3,000 metres high and called the Roof of Indochina.

items.q: Which hill city is known as the City of Eternal Spring?
items.h: Đà Lạt sits high in the hills, so it stays cool all year and is full of flowers.

items.q: What kind of dish is Vietnamese phở?
items.h: Phở is noodle soup in a rich broth, usually with beef or chicken and fresh herbs.

items.q: Bánh mì is a Vietnamese sandwich made with which bread?
items.h: Bánh mì fills a crusty baguette with Vietnamese meats, pickles and fresh herbs.

items.q: Which square sticky rice cake is made for Tết?
items.h: Bánh chưng is wrapped in green leaves, and its square shape stands for the Earth.

items.q: Bánh xèo is named after which sound it makes in the pan?
items.h: Bánh xèo is a crispy yellow pancake; 'xèo' is the sizzle of batter in a hot pan.

items.q: Vietnam's famous nước mắm sauce is made from what?
items.h: Nước mắm is made by packing small fish, like anchovies, in salt for many months.

items.q: In Vietnamese, what does 'xin chào' mean?
items.h: Xin chào is a friendly, polite way to say hello to anyone in Vietnamese.

items.q: In Vietnamese, what does 'cảm ơn' mean?
items.h: Cảm ơn means thank you, and cảm ơn nhiều means thank you very much.

items.q: What does 'mẹ' mean in Vietnamese?
items.h: Mẹ means mum. Dad is bố in the north of Vietnam and ba in the south.

items.q: What does the Vietnamese word 'ngon' mean?
items.h: When food is really delicious, Vietnamese people say 'ngon quá!' (so tasty!).

items.q: In Vietnamese, 'năm' means 'year' and which number?
items.h: Năm means both five and year, so 'năm năm' means five years!

items.q: What does 'lá' mean in nón lá, Vietnam's cone-shaped hat?
items.h: Nón lá means leaf hat: palm leaves on a bamboo frame keep off the sun and rain.

items.q: Which long tunic, worn over trousers, is Vietnam's national dress?
items.h: Áo dài means 'long shirt'; many people wear one for Tết, weddings and big days.

items.q: How many strings does the Vietnamese đàn bầu have?
items.h: The đàn bầu has one string; players bend its notes by moving a flexible rod.

items.q: Vietnam's water puppet shows began long ago in which kind of field?
items.h: Water puppet shows have been put on for over 900 years, first in flooded rice fields.

items.q: What is Tết, Vietnam's biggest festival?
items.h: Tết starts on the first day of the lunar year, usually in late January or February.

items.q: What colour are lì xì, the lucky-money envelopes given at Tết?
items.h: Red stands for luck and happiness in Vietnam, so lì xì envelopes are red and gold.

items.q: Which cakes do Vietnamese families share at the Mid-Autumn Festival?
items.h: At Tết Trung Thu, children parade with star-shaped lanterns under the full moon.

items.q: In legend, the Vietnamese people came from a dragon and a what?
items.h: Legend says the fairy Âu Cơ laid 100 eggs, which hatched into 100 children.

items.q: What colour is the star on Vietnam's flag?
items.h: Vietnam's flag is red with one big five-pointed yellow star in the middle.

items.q: What is the name of Vietnam's money?
items.h: Vietnam's high-value đồng banknotes are made of tough plastic, not paper.

items.q: Which big animal has helped Vietnamese farmers plough for centuries?
items.h: Water buffalo love wallowing in mud, which keeps them cool and protects their skin.

items.q: Which rare Vietnamese animal is nicknamed the Asian unicorn?
items.h: Scientists first discovered the saola, a shy forest animal with long horns, in 1992.

items.q: Hạ Long Bay is famous for tall islands made of which rock?
items.h: Over millions of years, rain and sea carved Hạ Long Bay's limestone into towers.

items.q: Phong Nha-Kẻ Bàng National Park is famous for its giant what?
items.h: Phong Nha-Kẻ Bàng has Sơn Đoòng, a cave so huge it has its own jungle and river.

items.q: The Mekong is Cửu Long in Vietnamese. What does that mean?
items.h: In Vietnam the Mekong splits into many branches, like dragons racing to the sea.

items.q: At Cái Răng in the Mekong Delta, the market takes place on what?
items.h: At floating markets, sellers hang fruit and veg on tall poles to show what they sell.

items.q: Which crop grows in Vietnam's wet paddy fields?
items.h: Rice plants grow with their roots under water in fields called paddies.

items.q: Sa Pa's hills are cut into rice terraces shaped like giant what?
items.h: Terraces turn steep hillsides into flat steps, so rice can be grown on them.

items.q: Hồ Chí Minh City is also known by which older name?
items.h: The river winding through Hồ Chí Minh City is still called the Saigon River.

items.q: What does 'trứng' mean in cà phê trứng, Hà Nội's famous coffee?
items.h: Cà phê trứng is strong coffee topped with a sweet cream of whipped egg yolk.

items.q: Which animal is the hero of the legend of Hoàn Kiếm Lake?
items.h: Hoàn Kiếm means 'returned sword': a golden turtle took a magic sword back.

items.q: Hà Nội's old name, Thăng Long, means 'rising' what?
items.h: In 1010 King Lý Thái Tổ named the city after a dragon he saw flying up into the sky.

items.q: Hà Nội's Temple of Literature was home to Vietnam's first what?
items.h: Vietnam's first university opened there in 1076; stone turtles carry top scholars' names.

items.q: Hà Nội's One Pillar Pagoda is shaped like which flower?
items.h: The lotus grows in muddy ponds yet blooms clean, so it is loved all over Vietnam.

items.q: Which of these countries shares a border with Vietnam?
items.h: Vietnam has three land neighbours: China, Laos and Cambodia.

items.q: Vietnam's long, curvy shape looks like which letter?
items.h: Vietnam is S-shaped, with a coastline more than 3,000 kilometres long.

items.q: The Mekong River reaches the sea in which country?
items.h: The Mekong flows through six countries before reaching the sea in Vietnam's delta.

items.q: Vạn Phúc village near Hà Nội is famous for weaving what?
items.h: Silk thread comes from the cocoons of silkworms, which feed on mulberry leaves.

items.q: Bát Tràng village near Hà Nội is famous for making what?
items.h: Bát Tràng potters have shaped clay into bowls, vases and teapots for centuries.

items.q: In Vietnam's zodiac, which animal takes the rabbit's place?
items.h: Vietnam's zodiac has 12 animals, like China's, but with the Cat instead of the Rabbit.

items.q: How many tones does standard Vietnamese have?
items.h: With six tones, ma, má, mà, mả, mã and mạ are all different words!

items.q: Hà Nội's Old Quarter is famous as the place of 36 what?
items.h: Many Old Quarter streets are named after what they sold, like Hàng Bạc for silver.

items.q: What is Vietnam's biggest island?
items.h: Phú Quốc, in Vietnam's far south-west, is famous for its pepper and fish sauce.

items.q: Which is the largest continent?
items.h: Asia is the biggest continent, covering almost a third of all the land on Earth.

items.q: Which ocean lies between Europe and North America?
items.h: The Atlantic grows a few centimetres wider every year as its sea floor spreads.

items.q: Which ocean surrounds the North Pole?
items.h: The Arctic is the smallest ocean, and much of it is covered in floating sea ice.

items.q: On which continent is the South Pole?
items.h: Antarctica is the coldest, windiest continent, covered by a huge sheet of ice.

items.q: What is the capital of France?
items.h: Paris sits on the River Seine, and more than 30 bridges cross the river in the city.

items.q: What is the capital of Japan?
items.h: Tokyo means 'eastern capital', and its old name was Edo.

items.q: What is the capital of Italy?
items.h: Legend says Rome was founded nearly 2,800 years ago by twins raised by a wolf.

items.q: What is the capital of Egypt?
items.h: Cairo sits on the River Nile, close to the great pyramids of Giza.

items.q: What is the capital of Australia?
items.h: Canberra was built as a new capital because Sydney and Melbourne both wanted to be it.

items.q: What is the capital of China?
items.h: Beijing means 'northern capital', and parts of the Great Wall are close to the city.

items.q: What is the capital of Brazil?
items.h: Brasília was built in the late 1950s, and from above its plan looks like an aeroplane.

items.q: What is the capital of Scotland?
items.h: Edinburgh Castle stands on Castle Rock, the remains of an ancient volcano.

items.q: What is the capital of Wales?
items.h: The Welsh flag shows a red dragon on a green and white background.

items.q: Which river flows through London?
items.h: The River Thames starts in the Cotswolds and flows through London to the North Sea.

items.q: What is the highest mountain in the UK?
items.h: Ben Nevis in Scotland is 1,345 metres high, and its top is often covered in snow.

items.q: Which is the highest mountain on Earth?
items.h: Mount Everest, in the Himalayas, rises nearly 9 kilometres above sea level.

items.q: Which mountains run down the west side of South America?
items.h: Llamas and alpacas come from the high, chilly Andes mountains.

items.q: Which mountains are famous for skiing in Switzerland?
items.h: The Alps stretch across eight countries, including France, Italy and Austria.

items.q: What is the largest hot desert in the world?
items.h: The Sahara covers much of North Africa and is almost as big as the whole USA.

items.q: On which continent is the Gobi Desert?
items.h: The Gobi is a cold desert, and famous dinosaur eggs have been dug up there.

items.q: Which great river flows through Egypt?
items.h: Ancient Egyptians farmed the rich black mud the Nile left on its banks each year.

items.q: Most of the Amazon rainforest is in which country?
items.h: The Amazon River carries more water into the sea than any other river.

items.q: Which country has a red maple leaf on its flag?
items.h: Maple syrup is made from the sweet sap of maple trees, collected in early spring.

items.q: What colour is the circle on Japan's flag?
items.h: Japan's flag shows a red sun on white; Japan is called the Land of the Rising Sun.

items.q: Which country is shaped like a boot?
items.h: Italy looks like a boot kicking a ball, and the 'ball' is the island of Sicily.

items.q: On which continent is Peru?
items.h: Peru is home to Machu Picchu, an Inca city built high in the Andes mountains.

items.q: Which sea lies between Europe and Africa?
items.h: Mediterranean means 'in the middle of the land', as land surrounds the sea.

items.q: In which country is the Grand Canyon?
items.h: The Colorado River carved the Grand Canyon over millions of years.

items.q: On which continent is Mount Kilimanjaro?
items.h: Kilimanjaro, in Tanzania, is a giant volcano and the highest mountain in Africa.

items.q: Which ocean lies between Africa and Australia?
items.h: The Indian Ocean is the only ocean named after a country: India.

items.q: At what temperature does pure water freeze?
items.h: Water expands as it freezes, so ice is lighter than water and floats.

items.q: At what temperature does water boil at sea level?
items.h: Boiling water turns into an invisible gas called water vapour.

items.q: What is it called when a liquid turns into a gas?
items.h: Puddles dry up after rain because the water slowly evaporates into the air.

items.q: What is it called when a gas cools and turns into a liquid?
items.h: Condensation is why a glass of cold juice gets drops of water on the outside.

items.q: Which of these is a gas at room temperature?
items.h: Oxygen has no colour or smell, and we need it in every breath we take.

items.q: Which state of matter keeps its own shape?
items.h: Solids keep their shape, liquids take the shape of their container and gases spread out.

items.q: Which of these metals is attracted to a magnet?
items.h: Iron, nickel and cobalt are magnetic, but most metals, like copper, are not.

items.q: What do two magnets' north poles do when pushed together?
items.h: Like poles push each other away, while opposite poles pull together.

items.q: Which force pulls things down towards the Earth?
items.h: Gravity keeps our feet on the ground and holds the Moon in orbit around the Earth.

items.q: Which force slows a bike down when you squeeze the brakes?
items.h: Friction happens when surfaces rub together, and it can make them warm up.

items.q: Which force pushes up on a boat to help it float?
items.h: Water pushes up on a boat with a force called upthrust, which helps it stay afloat.

items.q: Light travels in what kind of lines?
items.h: Light travels in straight lines, so it cannot bend round things in its way.

items.q: What forms when an object blocks light?
items.h: Shadows are longest in the early morning and evening, when the Sun is low in the sky.

items.q: What do objects do to make a sound?
items.h: Touch your throat while you hum, and you can feel your voice box vibrating.

items.q: Which of these can sound NOT travel through?
items.h: Space is silent because there is no air for sound vibrations to travel through.

items.q: What do we call a sound bouncing back off a wall?
items.h: Bats and dolphins find their way using echoes of the sounds they make.

items.q: Which of these materials lets electricity flow through it?
items.h: Copper is a good conductor, so it is used for the wires inside electric cables.

items.q: What is a material that does not let electricity through called?
items.h: Plastic is a good insulator, so it is wrapped around wires to keep us safe.

items.q: For a bulb to light, what must its circuit be?
items.h: A switch makes a gap in the circuit, so electricity stops flowing and the bulb goes out.

items.q: What do we call a material you can see clearly through?
items.h: Glass is transparent, frosted glass is translucent, and wood is opaque.

items.q: What happens to sugar when you stir it into warm water?
items.h: Sugar dissolves rather than melts: it spreads through the water and makes it sweet.

items.q: Iron rusts when it meets water and which gas?
items.h: Rust is a flaky orange-brown layer that forms on iron left out in damp air.

items.q: What colour does light make when all the rainbow's colours mix?
items.h: Sunlight looks white, but a prism splits it into all the colours of the rainbow.

items.q: What unit is force measured in?
items.h: Forces are measured in newtons, named after the scientist Isaac Newton.

items.q: A seesaw is an example of which simple machine?
items.h: A lever turns on a point called a fulcrum, helping you lift heavy loads more easily.

items.q: Which simple machine uses a rope over a wheel to lift loads?
items.h: Cranes use pulleys, so a smaller pull can lift a much heavier load.

items.q: What is the chemical formula for water?
items.h: Each tiny bit of water is two hydrogen atoms joined to one oxygen atom.

items.q: Diamonds and pencil 'lead' are both made of which element?
items.h: Pencil 'lead' is really graphite, a soft form of carbon; diamond is a hard form.

items.q: Which planet is closest to the Sun?
items.h: Mercury is the smallest planet and zooms around the Sun once every 88 days.

items.q: Which is the hottest planet in our solar system?
items.h: Venus is even hotter than Mercury because its thick clouds trap the Sun's heat.

items.q: Which is the largest planet in our solar system?
items.h: Jupiter is so big that more than 1,000 Earths could fit inside it.

items.q: Which planet is famous for its bright, wide rings?
items.h: Saturn's rings are made of billions of chunks of ice and rock.

items.q: Which planet have the Curiosity and Perseverance rovers explored?
items.h: Mars looks red because its soil is full of rusty iron dust.

items.q: How long does Earth take to travel once around the Sun?
items.h: Earth's trip round the Sun takes about 365 and a quarter days, so we have leap years.

items.q: How long does Earth take to spin round once?
items.h: As Earth spins, your side turns towards the Sun for day and away from it for night.

items.q: What is the Sun?
items.h: The Sun is a star, a giant ball of hot gas, and the closest star to Earth.

items.q: Roughly how long does sunlight take to reach Earth?
items.h: Sunlight travels about 150 million km to reach us in just over 8 minutes.

items.q: Who was the first person to walk on the Moon?
items.h: Neil Armstrong stepped onto the Moon in 1969; with no wind there, footprints last ages.

items.q: Who was the first person to travel into space?
items.h: Yuri Gagarin flew once around the Earth in 1961 in a spacecraft called Vostok 1.

items.q: Who was the first British person to go into space?
items.h: Helen Sharman, a chemist from Sheffield, visited the Mir space station in 1991.

items.q: What kind of spacecraft is the ISS?
items.h: Astronauts on the International Space Station see about 16 sunrises every day.

items.q: What do we call a space rock that lands on Earth?
items.h: Shooting stars are space rocks burning up in the air; any that land are meteorites.

items.q: What is a comet mostly made of?
items.h: Comets are 'dirty snowballs'; near the Sun their ice turns to gas and makes a tail.

items.q: Which planet spins tipped over on its side?
items.h: Uranus is tipped right over, so it rolls round the Sun like a ball.

items.q: Which planet is furthest from the Sun?
items.h: Neptune is so far away that one trip round the Sun takes about 165 Earth years.

items.q: What type of space object is Pluto?
items.h: In 2006, scientists decided that Pluto is a dwarf planet, not a full planet.

items.q: How many planets are in our solar system?
items.h: The planets are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

items.q: What is the name of our galaxy?
items.h: The Milky Way is a giant spiral of stars, and our Sun is just one of billions.

items.q: Where does moonlight really come from?
items.h: The Moon makes no light of its own; it shines by reflecting light from the Sun.

items.q: How long does the Moon take to go through all its phases?
items.h: The Moon goes from new to full and back again in about 29 and a half days.

items.q: What is a group of stars that makes a pattern in the sky called?
items.h: Orion, the Hunter, is a constellation with three bright stars in a row as his belt.

items.q: What is the path of a planet around the Sun called?
items.h: Every planet travels around the Sun in an orbit shaped like a slightly squashed circle.

items.q: What is it called when the Moon blocks the Sun's light?
items.h: In a total solar eclipse the day goes dark. Never look straight at the Sun!

items.q: What made most of the round craters on the Moon?
items.h: Space rocks smashed into the Moon, and with no wind or rain the craters stay for ages.

items.q: What is the fastest land animal?
items.h: A cheetah can reach about 100 km per hour, but only in short bursts.

items.q: What is the largest animal alive today?
items.h: Blue whales can grow to about 30 metres long, yet they feed on tiny shrimp-like krill.

items.q: What is the tallest animal?
items.h: A giraffe's long neck has just seven bones, the same number as a human's neck.

items.q: What is a baby kangaroo called?
items.h: A newborn joey is about the size of a jelly bean and grows in its mum's pouch.

items.q: What is a baby frog called?
items.h: Tadpoles hatch in water and breathe with gills before growing legs and lungs.

items.q: What is a baby swan called?
items.h: Fluffy grey cygnets sometimes ride on their parents' backs to keep warm and safe.

items.q: What do we call an animal that eats only plants?
items.h: Cows, rabbits and elephants are herbivores; they munch plants all day long.

items.q: What do we call an animal that eats both plants and meat?
items.h: Bears, pigs and humans are omnivores, eating both plants and animals.

items.q: Which of these animals is a mammal?
items.h: Dolphins breathe air through a blowhole and feed their babies on milk.

items.q: Which of these is NOT an insect?
items.h: Spiders are arachnids with eight legs, like scorpions, ticks and mites.

items.q: How many legs does an insect have?
items.h: Every insect has six legs and three body parts: head, thorax and abdomen.

items.q: Which group of animals has feathers?
items.h: Birds are the only animals alive today with feathers, used for flying and warmth.

items.q: What do fish use to breathe under water?
items.h: Gills take in oxygen from the water as it flows over them.

items.q: Where do polar bears live in the wild?
items.h: Polar bears live around the North Pole, while most penguins live far to the south.

items.q: Which sea animal can change colour in a flash to hide?
items.h: An octopus has three hearts and can change its colour in less than a second.

items.q: What is a group of lions called?
items.h: In a pride, the lionesses do most of the hunting, working together as a team.

items.q: Which of these animals is a marsupial?
items.h: Koalas carry their babies in a pouch and eat almost nothing but eucalyptus leaves.

items.q: What is a butterfly's resting stage after being a caterpillar?
items.h: Inside its chrysalis, a caterpillar's body is rebuilt into a butterfly.

items.q: Which bird is famous for copying human speech?
items.h: Parrots copy sounds they hear, and some African grey parrots learn hundreds of words.

items.q: What makes flamingos pink?
items.h: Flamingos get their pink colour from the tiny shrimps and algae they eat.

items.q: Which sense does a snake's flicking tongue help with?
items.h: A snake flicks its tongue to pick up smells from the air around it.

items.q: What do honeybees make from flower nectar?
items.h: A single honeybee makes only about a twelfth of a teaspoon of honey in its life.

items.q: Which animal sleeps hanging upside down?
items.h: Bats are the only mammals that can truly fly, and many roost upside down in caves.

items.q: What do giant pandas eat most of the time?
items.h: Giant pandas spend around half of every day munching bamboo.

items.q: Which of these animals is a reptile?
items.h: Reptiles have dry, scaly skin, and most of them lay eggs on land.

items.q: What is stored in a camel's hump?
items.h: A camel's hump stores fat, which it can use for energy when food is hard to find.

items.q: Which animal builds dams across rivers?
items.h: Beavers gnaw through trees with strong orange teeth and build dams of sticks and mud.

items.q: Which animal lives in an underground home called a sett?
items.h: Badgers live in setts; foxes live in dens, rabbits in warrens and squirrels in dreys.

items.q: How many bones are in an adult human body?
items.h: Babies are born with around 300 bones, and some join together as they grow.

items.q: What is the longest bone in your body?
items.h: Your thigh bone, the femur, is the longest and strongest bone in your body.

items.q: Where is the smallest bone in your body?
items.h: The stirrup bone, deep inside your ear, is smaller than a grain of rice.

items.q: Which bones make a cage around your heart and lungs?
items.h: Most people have 12 pairs of ribs, which protect the heart and lungs.

items.q: Which bone protects your brain?
items.h: Your skull is made of many bones that fit together like a jigsaw.

items.q: Which organ is a muscle that beats all day and all night?
items.h: Your heart is a strong muscle about the size of your fist.

items.q: Which organs do you use to breathe?
items.h: Your lungs take in oxygen from the air and breathe out carbon dioxide.

items.q: Which organ controls your whole body?
items.h: Your brain sends messages along nerves to every part of your body in a split second.

items.q: What is the largest organ of the human body?
items.h: Your skin is your largest organ; it keeps germs out and helps you stay cool.

items.q: Which organs take waste out of your body to make wee?
items.h: You have two kidneys, each about the size of a fist, tucked under your ribs.

items.q: Which organ churns your food with strong juices?
items.h: Your stomach mixes food with strong acid to help break it down.

items.q: How many teeth are in a full set of adult teeth?
items.h: Children have 20 baby teeth, which are replaced by a full adult set of 32.

items.q: Which of the five senses does your nose give you?
items.h: Your nose can tell apart thousands of different smells.

items.q: What is the coloured part of your eye called?
items.h: The iris is a ring of muscle that makes the black pupil bigger or smaller.

items.q: What do muscles do to move your bones?
items.h: Muscles can only pull, so they work in pairs, like the biceps and triceps in your arm.

items.q: What do we call the places where bones meet and bend?
items.h: Joints are where bones meet; your knees and elbows bend like door hinges.

items.q: Which joint lets your arm swing round in a big circle?
items.h: The shoulder is a ball-and-socket joint, so it can move in almost every direction.

items.q: Which vitamin does your skin make in sunshine?
items.h: Vitamin D is called the sunshine vitamin, and it helps keep your bones strong.

items.q: How many hours of sleep do children of 9 or 10 need each night?
items.h: Sleep helps your body grow and your brain store what you learned today.

items.q: Bread, rice and pasta are full of which energy food?
items.h: Carbohydrates give you the energy to run, play and think.

items.q: Which food group helps your muscles grow and repair?
items.h: Eggs, beans, fish and meat are full of protein for strong muscles.

items.q: How long should you brush your teeth for each time?
items.h: Dentists say brush for two minutes, twice a day, with fluoride toothpaste.

items.q: What are the small bones that make up your spine called?
items.h: Your spine is a stack of small bones called vertebrae, which let you bend and twist.

items.q: Where are most of your taste buds?
items.h: Taste buds sense sweet, salty, sour, bitter and savoury flavours.

items.q: What is the hard, white outer layer of a tooth called?
items.h: Tooth enamel is the hardest stuff in your body, even harder than bone.

items.q: Over half of your bones are in which parts of your body?
items.h: Your two hands and two feet together hold 106 of your 206 bones.

items.q: Which gas do plants take in from the air to make their food?
items.h: Plants use sunlight, water and carbon dioxide to make food, and give out oxygen.

items.q: Which part of a plant takes in water from the soil?
items.h: Roots soak up water and hold the plant firmly in the ground.

items.q: What green substance in leaves captures sunlight?
items.h: Chlorophyll uses sunlight to help a plant turn water and air into food.

items.q: What is it called when pollen moves from flower to flower?
items.h: Bees, butterflies and the wind carry pollen between flowers so seeds can form.

items.q: What is it called when a seed starts to grow?
items.h: A seed needs water, air and warmth to germinate; many do not even need light.

items.q: What are trees that lose their leaves in autumn called?
items.h: Deciduous trees like oak drop their leaves in autumn; evergreens like holly keep them.

items.q: In the water cycle, what forms when water vapour cools in the sky?
items.h: Clouds are made of billions of tiny water droplets or ice crystals.

items.q: What is rain, snow, sleet or hail called in the water cycle?
items.h: After precipitation, water runs into rivers and seas, and the cycle starts again.

items.q: What powers the water cycle?
items.h: The Sun's heat makes water evaporate from seas and lakes, starting the water cycle.

items.q: What is molten rock called once it pours out of a volcano?
items.h: Molten rock is called magma while it is underground and lava once it comes out.

items.q: Which of these rocks forms when lava cools?
items.h: Basalt is an igneous rock; the Giant's Causeway is made of basalt columns.

items.q: What do we call the remains of ancient life found in rock?
items.h: Mary Anning found amazing fossils on the beaches of Lyme Regis over 200 years ago.

items.q: Chalk and limestone are which type of rock?
items.h: Chalk is made from the tiny shells of sea plankton that lived millions of years ago.

items.q: What is a huge, slow-moving river of ice called?
items.h: Glaciers creep slowly downhill, carving deep U-shaped valleys as they go.

items.q: What is a scientist who studies the weather called?
items.h: Meteorologists use satellites and weather balloons to forecast the weather.

items.q: What do we call the usual weather of a place over many years?
items.h: Weather changes from day to day, but climate is the pattern over many years.

items.q: What does a weather vane show?
items.h: A weather vane points into the wind; an anemometer measures how fast it blows.

items.q: In which season do many leaves turn orange and red?
items.h: In autumn, trees stop making green chlorophyll, so the leaves' other colours show.

items.q: What is at the start of almost every food chain?
items.h: Plants are producers: they make their own food using sunlight.

items.q: In a food chain, what is an animal that hunts others called?
items.h: In the food chain grass → rabbit → fox, the fox is the predator and the rabbit is prey.

items.q: What is the natural home of an animal or plant called?
items.h: Habitats include rainforests, deserts, ponds and oceans, each suiting different life.

items.q: Which habitat gets very little rain all year round?
items.h: Deserts can be hot or cold: Antarctica counts as a desert because so little snow falls.

items.q: What is the thick, leafy 'roof' of a rainforest called?
items.h: The canopy is so thick that very little sunlight reaches the rainforest floor.

items.q: A rainbow forms when sunlight shines through what?
items.h: Raindrops split sunlight into colours, with red on the outside and violet inside.

items.q: Bamboo is actually a giant kind of what?
items.h: Bamboo is a grass, and some kinds can grow over half a metre in a single day.

items.q: Which tree do acorns grow on?
items.h: A big old oak tree can drop thousands of acorns in a single year.

items.q: What is a long, deep winter sleep called?
items.h: In the UK, hedgehogs, dormice and bats hibernate through the cold winter.

items.q: What is a huge floating chunk of ice at sea called?
items.h: About nine-tenths of an iceberg is hidden under the water.

items.q: Which ancient people built the pyramids at Giza?
items.h: The Great Pyramid of Giza was built about 4,500 years ago for the pharaoh Khufu.

items.q: What was the title of a king of ancient Egypt?
items.h: Tutankhamun became pharaoh when he was only about nine years old.

items.q: What is the picture writing of ancient Egypt called?
items.h: Hieroglyphs used little pictures, and the Rosetta Stone helped experts read them again.

items.q: In which country did the Olympic Games begin?
items.h: The first Olympic Games we know of were held at Olympia, Greece, in 776 BC.

items.q: What did winners at the ancient Olympics get?
items.h: Ancient Olympic winners were crowned with a wreath of olive leaves, not a medal.

items.q: Which language did the ancient Romans speak?
items.h: Many English words come from Latin, like 'aqua' (water), which gave us 'aquarium'.

items.q: What did the Romans build to carry water to their towns?
items.h: Roman aqueducts sloped gently downhill so water could flow for many kilometres.

items.q: Which Roman emperor's wall stretches across northern England?
items.h: Hadrian's Wall, begun in AD 122, ran about 117 km from coast to coast.

items.q: Whose team was the first to reach the South Pole, in 1911?
items.h: Roald Amundsen's Norwegian team reached the South Pole with dogs pulling sledges.

items.q: Who first reached the top of Everest with Tenzing Norgay?
items.h: Edmund Hillary, from New Zealand, and Tenzing Norgay, a Sherpa, did it in 1953.

items.q: Which British scientist invented the World Wide Web?
items.h: Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web in 1989 and let everyone use it for free.

items.q: What powered the first railway locomotives?
items.h: George Stephenson's Rocket, built in 1829, is one of the most famous steam engines.

items.q: In 1783, what did the first people to fly travel in?
items.h: Before people flew, a sheep, a duck and a rooster rode in a Montgolfier hot-air balloon.

items.q: Which scientist studied finches on the Galápagos Islands?
items.h: Charles Darwin noticed that finches on different islands had differently shaped beaks.

items.q: In which country is the Great Wall?
items.h: It's a myth that you can see the Great Wall from the Moon with just your eyes.

items.q: In which country is Stonehenge?
items.h: Some of Stonehenge's stones were brought about 240 km from hills in Wales.

items.q: Which engineer designed the Clifton Suspension Bridge?
items.h: Isambard Kingdom Brunel also built the SS Great Britain, an early iron steamship.

items.q: What did the Romans call London?
items.h: The Romans founded Londinium almost 2,000 years ago, beside the River Thames.

items.q: What did Alexander Graham Bell patent in 1876?
items.h: Bell, born in Edinburgh, made his first phone call to his assistant, Mr Watson.

items.q: What did John Logie Baird first show the public in 1926?
items.h: Scottish inventor John Logie Baird showed moving pictures on a TV screen in London.

items.q: Which tower was built in Paris for a world's fair in 1889?
items.h: The Eiffel Tower was only meant to stand for 20 years, but Paris kept it.

items.q: What did Archimedes shout in his bath, so the story goes?
items.h: Eureka is Greek for 'I have found it!'; he'd worked out how to measure volume.

items.q: Who was the first person to win two Nobel Prizes?
items.h: Marie Curie won Nobel Prizes in both physics and chemistry for her work on radioactivity.

items.q: Who is often called the first computer programmer?
items.h: In 1843, Ada Lovelace wrote steps for Charles Babbage's planned computing machine.

items.q: Which direction-finding tool was invented in ancient China?
items.h: Early Chinese compasses were magnetic spoons that turned to point south.

items.q: Who built a famous printing press in Germany around 1450?
items.h: Gutenberg's press could print pages far faster than copying books out by hand.

items.q: What did Joseph Swan and Thomas Edison both make in the 1870s?
items.h: A light bulb glows when electricity heats a very thin wire called a filament.

items.q: What did Galileo build to study the night sky?
items.h: In 1610, Galileo used his telescope to spot four moons going round Jupiter.

items.q: Which festival of lights is famous for rangoli patterns and diyas?
items.h: At Diwali, families light small clay lamps called diyas and enjoy fireworks.

items.q: Which spring festival in India is famous for throwing coloured powder?
items.h: Holi welcomes spring with music, dancing and clouds of bright colour.

items.q: Which country holds a famous Carnival in Rio de Janeiro?
items.h: Rio's Carnival has huge parades of samba dancers in sparkly costumes.

items.q: In which country is hanami, cherry-blossom viewing, a spring custom?
items.h: In spring, families in Japan picnic under pink cherry blossom; this is called hanami.

items.q: What is sushi usually made with?
items.h: Sushi is Japanese rice flavoured with vinegar, often with raw fish or vegetables.

items.q: Which Italian city is famous as the home of pizza?
items.h: The Margherita pizza shows the colours of Italy's flag: red, white and green.

items.q: Which country is famous for tacos and tortillas?
items.h: Tortillas are flatbreads made from maize or wheat, and a taco is a folded tortilla.

items.q: Which country does paella come from?
items.h: Paella is a rice dish from Valencia, cooked in a wide, shallow pan.

items.q: Croissants are a famous breakfast in which country?
items.h: Croissant means 'crescent' in French, after its curved shape.

items.q: How many players does a football team have on the pitch?
items.h: A football team has 11 players on the pitch, and one of them is the goalkeeper.

items.q: In which sport do players score a try?
items.h: In rugby, players score a try by touching the ball down over the try line.

items.q: Which sport is played at Wimbledon?
items.h: Wimbledon was first played in 1877, and fans love eating strawberries and cream there.

items.q: How many rings are on the Olympic flag?
items.h: The five linked rings stand for five parts of the world meeting at the Games.

items.q: Which group has strings, woodwind, brass and percussion?
items.h: A conductor uses a thin stick called a baton to keep the orchestra together.

items.q: Which instrument usually has 88 black and white keys?
items.h: Pressing a piano key makes a little hammer hit strings inside the piano.

items.q: Which instrument is usually played with a bow?
items.h: The violin is the smallest and highest-sounding string instrument in an orchestra.

items.q: Which family of instruments does the trumpet belong to?
items.h: Brass players make sound by buzzing their lips into a cup-shaped mouthpiece.

items.q: Which instrument is famous in Scotland?
items.h: A piper blows air into a bag, then squeezes it to keep the pipes playing.

items.q: The didgeridoo comes from which country?
items.h: Aboriginal Australians have played the long, hollow wooden didgeridoo for centuries.

items.q: Who painted the Mona Lisa?
items.h: Leonardo da Vinci painted the Mona Lisa; it hangs in the Louvre museum in Paris.

items.q: Who painted 'The Starry Night' and bright sunflowers?
items.h: Vincent van Gogh used thick, swirly brushstrokes and bold yellows and blues.

items.q: How do you say 'hello' in Spanish?
items.h: Spanish is spoken in Spain and in most countries of South and Central America.

items.q: What is origami?
items.h: Origami is the Japanese art of folding paper, and a famous design is the paper crane.

items.q: Which board game has kings, queens, rooks and knights?
items.h: Chess began in India about 1,500 years ago, and the queen is its strongest piece.

items.q: Which sport uses a shuttlecock?
items.h: A shuttlecock has feathers or a plastic skirt, and players hit it over a high net.

items.q: Which short Japanese poem has 17 syllables?
items.h: A haiku has three lines of 5, 7 and 5 syllables, often about nature.

items.q: Which language do most people in Brazil speak?
items.h: Brazil is the only country in South America where Portuguese is the main language.

items.q: What is Scotland's New Year's Eve celebration called?
items.h: At Hogmanay, people join hands and sing Auld Lang Syne as the new year begins.

items.q: What is the Roman numeral for 50?
items.h: Roman numerals: I is 1, V is 5, X is 10, L is 50, C is 100, D is 500 and M is 1,000.

items.q: What number does the Roman numeral XIV stand for?
items.h: A smaller numeral before a bigger one is taken away, so IV is 4 and XIV is 14.

items.q: How is the number 2026 written in Roman numerals?
items.h: M is 1,000, so MM is 2,000; then XX is 20 and VI is 6.

items.q: How many degrees are in a right angle?
items.h: A right angle is a quarter turn, like the corner of a book.

items.q: How many degrees are in a full turn?
items.h: Spinning all the way round once is a full turn of 360 degrees.

items.q: Angles on a straight line add up to how many degrees?
items.h: A straight line is a half turn, so the angles along it always total 180 degrees.

items.q: What do the three angles inside any triangle add up to?
items.h: Tear the corners off a paper triangle and they fit together along a straight line!

items.q: What do we call an angle smaller than a right angle?
items.h: Acute angles are less than 90°, and obtuse angles are between 90° and 180°.

items.q: What is a triangle with all three sides equal called?
items.h: An equilateral triangle has three equal sides and three equal angles of 60°.

items.q: How many sides does a hexagon have?
items.h: Bees build honeycomb from hexagons, which fit together with no gaps.

items.q: How many edges does a cube have?
items.h: A cube has 6 square faces, 12 edges and 8 corners, called vertices.

items.q: What 3D shape is a tin of beans?
items.h: A cylinder has two flat circular faces and one curved face.

items.q: How many days are there in a leap year?
items.h: Leap years usually come every 4 years and add 29 February to the calendar.

items.q: How many seconds are there in an hour?
items.h: 60 seconds × 60 minutes = 3,600 seconds in every hour.

items.q: How many weeks are there in a year?
items.h: A year has 52 weeks plus one extra day, or two in a leap year.

items.q: How many metres are there in a kilometre?
items.h: Kilo means a thousand, so a kilometre is 1,000 metres and a kilogram is 1,000 grams.

items.q: Which of these is a prime number?
items.h: A prime number has exactly two factors, 1 and itself; 15, 21 and 27 all have more.

items.q: What is 7 squared?
items.h: Squaring means multiplying a number by itself: 7 × 7 = 49.

items.q: What is one tenth written as a decimal?
items.h: One tenth is 1 of 10 equal parts, written as 0.1.

items.q: What do we call the distance all the way around a shape?
items.h: To find a rectangle's perimeter, add up the lengths of all four sides.

items.q: What is the distance across a circle through its centre called?
items.h: A circle's diameter is always twice as long as its radius.

items.q: How many lines of symmetry does a square have?
items.h: A square has 4 lines of symmetry: two across the middle and two corner to corner.

items.q: What is the value of the 7 in 4,725?
items.h: In 4,725, the 7 is in the hundreds column, so it is worth 700.

items.q: Which of these numbers is the largest?
items.h: Compare tenths first: 0.8 has 8 tenths, but 0.75 has only 7 tenths.

items.q: What is three quarters as a percentage?
items.h: Three quarters means 3 out of 4, the same as 75 out of 100, or 75%.

items.q: How many years are there in a century?
items.h: A decade is 10 years, a century is 100 years and a millennium is 1,000 years.

items.q: What is a seven-sided shape called?
items.h: The UK's 20p and 50p coins are seven-sided shapes with curved edges.

items.q: What is 3 pm on the 24-hour clock?
items.h: On the 24-hour clock, add 12 to afternoon times, so 3 pm becomes 15:00.
